parts.visual:
A founder pitches a VC: 'We are growing so fast! We spent $100 on Facebook ads to get one user, and that user paid us $20 this year.' The VC asks: 'How long will they stay a user?' The founder says: 'Probably a year.' The VC closes their notebook and leaves. The startup is literally paying $100 to make $20.

The Golden Ratio:
1. CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost): The total money spent on sales and marketing divided by the number of new customers acquired.
2. LTV (Lifetime Value): The total amount of pure profit a single customer will give you before they cancel their subscription.
3. The 3:1 Rule: In Silicon Valley, a healthy business must have an LTV to CAC ratio of at least 3 to 1. If it costs $100 to get a user, that user must eventually generate $300 in profit.
parts.audio: A startup is a machine. You put $1 into the machine through marketing, and you need $3 to come out the other side over the next few years. If you put $1 in and only $0.50 comes out, you are not a business; you are a charity subsidizing Facebook ads.

questions.question: A SaaS startup spends $10,000 on Google Ads in January and gets 100 new paying users. What is their CAC?
options: $100. (Total Marketing Spend divided by New Users). It costs this startup exactly $100 in advertising to acquire a single paying human. This is the baseline number they must overcome to be profitable.
questions.correct_answer: $100. (Total Marketing Spend divided by New Users). It costs this startup exactly $100 in advertising to acquire a single paying human. This is the baseline number they must overcome to be profitable.
questions.explanation: You must know exactly how much you are paying to 'buy' a user.

questions.question: Listen to the VC criticizing a pitch. Why does the VC think the LTV calculation is a lie?
questions.tts_text: You are telling me your Lifetime Value is $5,000 per user because they pay $100 a month and you assume they will stay for 50 months. Your company is only 3 months old! You have no idea if they will stay for 50 months. You are guessing.
options: Fake Extrapolation. Early-stage founders often hallucinate their LTV by assuming users will stay forever. Until you have actual historical data proving that a user stays for 4 years, your LTV is just a dangerous theoretical guess.
questions.correct_answer: Fake Extrapolation. Early-stage founders often hallucinate their LTV by assuming users will stay forever. Until you have actual historical data proving that a user stays for 4 years, your LTV is just a dangerous theoretical guess.
questions.explanation: Hope is not a valid mathematical variable.

questions.question: A startup has an LTV/CAC ratio of 1:1 (It costs $100 to get a user, and the user generates $100 in profit). What happens if they raise $10 Million to scale?
options: They scale their own bankruptcy. If your unit economics are broken, raising VC money just allows you to lose money faster. You are pouring gasoline on a broken engine. You must fix the 1:1 ratio before you try to grow.
questions.correct_answer: They scale their own bankruptcy. If your unit economics are broken, raising VC money just allows you to lose money faster. You are pouring gasoline on a broken engine. You must fix the 1:1 ratio before you try to grow.
questions.explanation: Scaling a negative margin creates a massive crater.

questions.question: What is the 'Payback Period'?
options: The exact number of months it takes for a user to pay you back for their CAC. If CAC is $100, and they pay $10 a month, the payback period is 10 months. VCs want this to be under 12 months, or the startup requires too much cash to survive.
When the VC pays the founder.
